passage:
Lalit, you asked why your Mahima Bua always says "your feelings are information." It began when I was fourteen.
Three girls in my class sat behind me. One day they poured ink on my geography map and wrote a nasty word across it. "Arre, it was a joke. Can't you take a joke?" By the next week they were telling everyone it never happened, that I had spilled the ink myself.
I began to wonder. Maybe I did spill it. Maybe I am too touchy. I stopped telling Amma things, because what if I was wrong about those too?
Then our school librarian, Mrs D'Souza, found me crying between the shelves. I told her everything, expecting to hear I was overreacting. She said, "Ink does not write words by itself. What you felt was a real response to a real thing." That same afternoon she walked me to the class teacher and stayed while I told it again.

qa.q: What did the girls pour on young Mahima's geography map?
qa.a: They poured ink on her geography map and wrote a nasty word across it.

qa.q: What was young Mahima feeling when she began to wonder if she had spilled the ink herself?
qa.a: She felt confused and unsure of her own mind, afraid she was too touchy and might be wrong about other things too.

qa.q: At the turning point in the library, what choice helped young Mahima?
qa.a: She told Mrs D'Souza everything even though she expected to be dismissed, and hearing from someone outside the group helped her trust what she had seen and felt.

qa.q: How did Mrs D'Souza see what had happened?
qa.a: Mrs D'Souza saw it plainly as a real hurt, not an overreaction, and she acted that same afternoon by taking Mahima to the class teacher.

grounding: An aunt recalls how, at fourteen, classmates' claims that a cruel prank never happened made her doubt herself until a trusted adult outside the group confirmed what she saw.

passage:
Rain had turned the bus windows white, and Usha still had her maths exam the next morning. She got off two stops early anyway and ran to Rashmi Mausi's tailoring shop.
At dinner the night before, in front of the whole family, Mummy had called Usha "the slow one, not like her cousin". This morning, when Usha said it had hurt, Mummy frowned. "I never said that. You always make things up to feel sad." Papa only said, "Let it go, beta."
By lunch Usha was wondering if she had heard wrong.
Mausi pulled the shutter halfway down against the rain and listened without interrupting. Then she said, "Pooja told me about that dinner on the phone. You heard it right, and it's okay that it hurt. I'll speak to your Mummy gently this weekend."
Usha let out a breath she felt she had held all day. Mausi made tea and helped with two maths problems while the rain slowed.

qa.q: What exam did Usha have the next morning?
qa.a: Usha had her maths exam the next morning.

qa.q: Why did Usha let out a breath she felt she had held all day?
qa.a: She felt relief, because Mausi confirmed she had heard right and that her hurt made sense, easing a day of doubt.

qa.q: Why was getting off the bus to see Rashmi Mausi a wise choice, despite the rain and the exam?
qa.a: Talking to a trusted adult outside the dinner table let Usha check her memory against someone else's, which helped her trust herself again.

qa.q: What would change if Papa had said "I heard it too" instead of "Let it go"?
qa.a: Usha would not have spent the day doubting herself; one person at home confirming it would have kept her trust in her own memory steady.

grounding: A girl whose mother denies a hurtful remark at dinner begins to doubt herself, and a trusted aunt outside the situation confirms what she heard.

passage:
In the small town, the girls walked home from school in a group, and for three weeks, they had walked a little faster when Lavanya caught up.
On Friday, Shreya, who had been her best friend since Class 1, said in front of all of them, "We're not leaving you out. You're imagining things. You're always so sensitive."
Lavanya began to wonder. Maybe she was sensitive. Maybe she'd imagined the whispers, the saved seats given to someone else, the laughter that stopped when she walked in.
That evening she went to her Bua's house on the next street, the one grown-up who wasn't part of any of it. She told her everything, in order.
Bua listened, then said, "Lavanya, you're not imagining it. Those are real things you saw. When someone says they didn't happen, it doesn't make them disappear."
Lavanya cried, and then slept properly for the first time in a week.

qa.q: Where did Lavanya go that evening?
qa.a: To her Bua's house on the next street.

qa.q: How was Lavanya feeling after Shreya called her sensitive?
qa.a: Lavanya felt hurt and confused, beginning to doubt whether she had imagined being left out.

qa.q: What helped Lavanya trust her own perception again?
qa.a: Talking to her Bua, a trusted adult outside the situation, who confirmed the things she saw were real.

qa.q: How might Shreya see what she said?
qa.a: Shreya may prefer to believe they aren't leaving Lavanya out, perhaps to avoid feeling guilty herself.

grounding: It shows a teenager told her exclusion is imagined, doubting herself, and regaining trust in her perception through a trusted adult outside the group.

passage:
At the Berlin secondary school, Elif had just moved from Istanbul. In the first week, Pablo imitated her accent in the corridor, loud and exaggerated. Everyone laughed. Elif's face burned.
The next day, she asked him to stop. Pablo looked surprised. "What? That was nothing. It was a joke. You weren't even upset. Don't be so dramatic." His friends nodded.
By the end of the week, Elif wasn't sure anymore. Had she been upset? Was she dramatic? Maybe she didn't understand German humour.
On Friday she went to the school counsellor, Frau Weber, who had nothing to do with the group. Elif told her, in careful German, exactly what happened.
Frau Weber nodded. "Elif, you felt humiliated. That's real. Someone calling it a joke afterwards doesn't change what you felt in that corridor."
Elif let out a long breath. For the first time in days, her own memory felt solid again.

qa.q: Who did Elif talk to on Friday?
qa.a: The school counsellor, Frau Weber.

qa.q: How did Elif feel by the end of the week?
qa.a: Elif felt confused and unsure, doubting whether she had really been upset after being told it was only a joke.

qa.q: What helped Elif restore trust in her own perception?
qa.a: Speaking to a trusted adult outside the group, who named her feeling as real and valid.

qa.q: How does Pablo see what he did?
qa.a: Pablo sees it as a harmless joke, perhaps to avoid facing that he hurt Elif.

grounding: It shows a teenager told a mocking moment was only a joke, doubting her feelings, and regaining trust in them through a counsellor outside the situation.

passage:
The school counsellor's room was quiet after lunch when Chandrika knocked.
"I don't know if this is even a real problem," she said. "Maybe I'm overreacting."
Last Thursday, Abhinav had sent a voice note to the class group mocking her stammer. She heard it. Then it was deleted. When she asked him about it, Abhinav and his friends said there was no voice note. "You must have dreamed it. Why would we do that?" By Monday, even her deskmate said, "Are you sure?"
"I keep thinking maybe I made it up," Chandrika whispered.
The counsellor pulled out a notebook. "Tell me exactly what you heard, when, and who else was in the group." Chandrika spoke slowly. The counsellor wrote it down.
"Chandrika, you're not overreacting. You heard it. I'll speak to the class teacher today and ask the group admin about deleted messages."
Chandrika left feeling steadier than she had in days.

qa.q: What did Abhinav's voice note mock?
qa.a: It was mocking her stammer.

qa.q: How was Chandrika feeling when she first knocked?
qa.a: Chandrika felt confused and doubtful, worried she was overreacting or had made it up.

qa.q: What did the counsellor do that helped?
qa.a: The counsellor listened, wrote down the details, confirmed Chandrika's experience, and said they would speak to the class teacher that day.

qa.q: How might Abhinav and his friends see the situation?
qa.a: They seem to want to deny it and avoid blame, pushing Chandrika to doubt what she heard.

grounding: It shows a teenager told that a mocking voice note never existed, doubting herself, and a counsellor outside the group helping restore trust in her perception.

passage:
Dear Masi,
Thank you for yesterday's call. I've been thinking about it all day.
For weeks I thought I was going mad. When Harish and the others put my old photo on the class group with that caption and everyone laughed, I cried in the washroom. The next day Harish said, "What photo? Nobody posted anything, you always twist things." The post was gone. By the end of the week even I wasn't sure. Maybe I was overreacting. Maybe it was a joke.
Then you asked me one question: what did you feel when you saw it? And I knew. I felt humiliated. That part didn't need proof.
You said I wasn't imagining it and it wasn't my fault, and before we hung up you helped me write to Ms Rao. She replied last night that she'll speak to the class and the counsellor today.
I feel steadier.
Love,
Anjali

qa.q: What did Harish say the next day?
qa.a: Harish said, “What photo? Nobody posted anything, you always twist things.”

qa.q: How did Anjali feel by the end of that week?
qa.a: Anjali felt confused and full of doubt, unsure whether the post had happened or whether it was overreacting to a joke.

qa.q: How did Masi's help work?
qa.a: Masi asked about Anjali's feelings, said it was not imagined and not Anjali's fault, and helped write to Ms Rao during that same call, bringing in someone who could act.

qa.q: What would change if Anjali had not spoken to anyone outside the class?
qa.a: Anjali might have kept doubting the memory, Harish's version could have become the only story, and nobody at school would have stepped in.

grounding: Shows a teenager told that a hurtful post never happened who begins doubting it, until a trusted adult outside the situation restores trust in their own perception.
